forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news.title: ‘This is the dream job’: Labour’s Bev Craig on the battle to be Greater Manchester mayor
news.summary:
Polling puts close Burnham ally in lead as she aims to defeat Reform and draw back support from revitalised Greens

Bev Craig was mid-squat at the gym when she was recognised for the first time as the prospective heir to Andy Burnham’s throne. Until recently, the Manchester city council leader could happily have gone about her workout in peace.

But all that changed when Burnham, who DJ’ed at her 40th birthday party last year, won the Makerfield byelection and set up another big electoral contest on his way to becoming prime minister.

news_drafts.headline: No lender acted on 29 September option to raise rates on Manchester's £340.7m of LOBO loans
news_drafts.lead:
No lender has moved to raise the interest rate on Manchester City Council's £340.7m of LOBO loans, according to the council's second-quarter treasury management report (its account of how it borrows and invests spare cash). A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. One such date passed on 29 September with no lender acting.

The loans carry rates above 4%. The report says: "Since the last report no lender has sought to exercise their option to date, one option passed on the 29th of September and there is one more this financial year on 26th of March."

The report goes to the Audit Committee on 13 October. If a lender does propose a higher rate on 26 March 2027, the council would have to choose between repaying the loan in full and accepting the new rate.

news_drafts.headline: Manchester forecasts £7.7m adult social care overspend after Care Closer to Home programme produced inconclusive benefit modelling
news_drafts.lead: Manchester Council is forecasting an overspend of £7.7m in adult social care by the end of the financial year, after a planned transformation programme failed to deliver expected savings. The council had budgeted for £2.5m in savings from a scheme called Care Closer to Home, which was meant to reduce costs, but the transformation has produced what the council's papers describe as "inconclusive benefit modelling"—meaning the savings cannot be measured or relied upon. The shortfall is driven by rising demand: the council is supporting 36 more people with complex learning disabilities than budgeted, 25 more in supported accommodation, and 44 additional mental health care packages. The papers note that unless the council finds new ways to cut costs or improve efficiency in-year, any further demand growth will push the overspend higher still.

findings.headline: LOBO call option date passed 29 September without lender exercise; next call date 26 March 2027 on £340.7m market loans held at rates above 4%
findings.detail: Council holds £340.7m of LOBO (lender option, borrower option) loans. One lender option date occurred on 29 September 2026 without the lender exercising the option to propose a higher rate. A second call date is scheduled for 26 March 2027. If a lender exercises, the council faces the choice to repay at par or accept a new (likely higher) rate.
findings.matters: LOBO calls are refinancing events; with rates at elevated levels, the risk of lender exercise is heightened; a call in March would force the council into a refinancing decision during a period of constrained capacity; a lender would want to know if the council has prepared for this scenario.
findings.figures: Market loans (LOBO) £340.7m; rates above 4%; call option occurred 29 Sept without exercise; next option 26 March 2027
findings.quote: Since the last report no lender has sought to exercise their option to date, one option passed on the 29th of September and there is one more this financial year on 26th of March.

findings.headline: Interest expenditure forecast to rise to £79.7m by 2028/29; net interest cost accelerating with interest income declining
findings.detail: Interest expenditure forecast to grow from £73.5m (2026/27) to £79.7m (2028/29) while interest income declines from £44.5m to £44.0m. The forecast net interest costs of £29.0m, £29.5m, and £35.7m respectively show accelerating growth in year 3. These shortfalls versus budget (£54.0m, £60.4m, £63.2m) are being covered by planned reserve drawdowns.
findings.matters: Rising net interest costs are consuming an increasing share of the council's revenue budget and the planned reserve; the trajectory shows accelerating cost pressure into 2029; another council watching peers would recognize this as a tightening revenue squeeze.
findings.figures: Interest expenditure £73.5m, £72.9m, £79.7m; Interest income £44.5m, £43.4m, £44.0m; Budget vs forecast shortfalls £9.0m, £6.4m, £14.0m
findings.quote: The increase in external borrowing alongside the expectation that on maturity any temporary borrowing will need refinancing means that the Council will pay more in external interest costs over the coming years.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Reserve forecast to decline by £29.4m over next three years to cover forecast budget shortfalls
findings.detail: Capital Financing Reserve stood at £106.0m at 31 March 2026. Forecast drawdowns of £9.0m in 2026/27, £6.4m in 2027/28, and £14.0m in 2028/29 are planned to cover interest and capital financing costs in excess of budget. The reserve is being consumed to sustain existing budget assumptions.
findings.matters: The reserve will be depleted by £29.4m (28% of current balance) in just three years; this limits capacity to absorb adverse variances or contingencies and indicates unsustainable budget structures; a lender would view reserve depletion as reducing the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: Reserve £106.0m at 31 March 2026; forecast drawdowns £9.0m, £6.4m, £14.0m; total decline £29.4m over three years
findings.quote: underspends from prior year's capital financing budgets have been transferred to the capital financing reserves, and now the Council is drawing down from these reserves.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing strategy depends on assumption that rates will fall significantly; temporary borrowing averages 4.48% against 3.81% benchmark, 67 basis points above market rates
findings.detail: The council deliberately borrows across short maturities (under 5 years) expecting to refinance when rates are lower. Temporary borrowing averaged £256.9m at 4.48%, or 67 basis points above the benchmark rate. If rates do not fall as forecast, this maturing debt will face expensive refinancing.
findings.matters: The strategy contains a directional bet on rate falls; with government rates already at 25-year highs and no guarantee of decline, the council faces material refinancing risk if rates remain elevated or rise; a lender would assess this as a risk to the council's future affordability.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing £256.9m average at 4.48%; benchmark 3.81%; spread 67bps; PWLB rates increased over period; gilts at 25-year highs
findings.quote: Under the TMSS, the strategy has been to borrow across a range of lower and relatively short-term maturities, for example less than 5 years, so that the debt can be refinanced at a point in time where longer term rates are expected to be significantly lower, driven by the assumptions that interest rates will fall from their current levels.

findings.headline: Interest rate forecasts now assume rates remain at current high levels longer than the February budget assumed; 10-year PWLB rates increased, gilts at 25-year highs
findings.detail: The council's February budget forecast assumed interest rates would fall significantly. September forecasts (now treating rates as stable longer term) represent a material deterioration. Over the same period, 10-year PWLB loan rates increased and government gilt rates reached their highest level in over 25 years at certain durations.
findings.matters: Budget affordability was built on rate-fall assumptions that have now weakened; if rates remain high rather than falling as budgeted, borrowing costs will exceed forecasts, tightening capital financing headroom and eroding the council's investment capacity.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB rates increased over period; government gilts 'highest for over 25 years at some durations'
findings.quote: It is worth noting that the interest rate forecasts shown in appendix C assume rates stay at current levels for longer than the rate forecast used in February when the budget was set.
